title: Any first rule of faith is logically indemonstrable
source_text: XIX. Imo ausim dicere ne quidem animo fingi posse ullum fidei fundamentum adversus quod non liceat similibus uti cavillationibus. Quicquid enim proferetur tanquam prima fidei regula, necesse est ut sit aliquid logice inevidens, & quod non possit proprie demonstrari. Nam principia fidei, ex communi Theologorum & Scholasticorum consensu, sunt inevidentia & indemonstrabilia. Ac praeterea necesse est ut non possit ex aliis fidei principiis tanquam prioribus & notioribus probari, alioqui prima regula non esset, sed daretur aliqua prior. Unde necessario sequitur primam fidei regulam, cujus authoritas quoad nos suprema est, esse aliquid quod argumentis de fide a priori probari non possit, & super quo etiam non possit satisfieri profanorum hominum quaestionibus per demonstrationes, & rationes prorsus necessarias atque evidentes.
pass_a_gloss: Indeed I would dare to say that not even in the mind can any foundation of faith be imagined against which it is not lawful to use similar cavils. For whatever is brought forward as the first rule of faith must be something logically inevident, and that cannot properly be demonstrated. For the principles of faith, by the common consent of Theologians and Scholastics, are inevident and indemonstrable. And besides it is necessary that it cannot be proved from other principles of faith as prior and better known; otherwise it would not be the first rule, but some prior one would be given. Whence it necessarily follows that the first rule of faith, whose authority as regards us is supreme, is something that cannot be proved by arguments of faith a priori, and about which also the questions of profane men cannot be satisfied by demonstrations and reasons altogether necessary and evident.
pass_b_english: I dare say one cannot even imagine a foundation of faith against which the same cavils would not be lawful.

Whatever is offered as faith's first rule must be something logically inevident and not properly demonstrable. Theologians and scholastics agree: the principles of faith are inevident and indemonstrable.
Nor can it be proved from other, prior, better-known principles of faith — or it would not be first, and some earlier rule would take its place.

So the first rule of faith, whose authority for us is supreme, cannot be proved by arguments of faith a priori, nor can the questions of irreligious men be met about it by demonstrations and strictly necessary, evident reasons.

lemmas.gloss: by arguments of faith a priori
